work.name: Client 01
work.line: A roofing firm that stopped losing jobs to the competitor down the road
work.challenge: Plenty of traffic from local ads, very few quote requests. The old site buried the phone number and asked for eleven fields before anyone could book a survey.
work.approach: We rebuilt the site around one action: booking a survey. A postcode checker sits on the homepage, the phone number is pinned to every screen, and the form asks for four things instead of eleven.
work.outcome: Quote requests more than tripled on the same ad spend, and the office now spends its mornings on callbacks instead of chasing half-finished forms.
work.quote: [A short quote from the client about the result.]

work.name: Client 02
work.line: A dental practice that moved booking out of the phone queue
work.challenge: New patients had to ring during opening hours to book, and most of the site traffic arrived in the evening.
work.approach: Online booking went on the homepage, treatment prices went public, and every treatment got its own page answering the questions reception was hearing on the phone.
work.outcome: New patient bookings went from eleven to forty-seven a month, most of them made outside opening hours.
work.quote: [A short quote from the client about the result.]

work.name: Client 03
work.line: A law firm that put its fees on the website
work.challenge: Every enquiry opened with the same question about price, and good prospects were leaving before asking it.
work.approach: Fixed fees went on every service page, each practice area got its own page, and the contact form went from eleven fields to four.
work.outcome: Completed enquiry forms rose 164% in ninety days, and the partners say first calls are shorter because the price conversation has already happened.
work.quote: [A short quote from the client about the result.]

work.name: Client 04
work.line: A landscaping company with a portfolio worth showing off
work.challenge: Their best work was sitting in a phone camera roll. The site showed three stock photos and attracted mostly small, price-sensitive jobs.
work.approach: A project-led site with a gallery that is easy to update from a phone, plus a guide to typical budgets so enquiries arrive with realistic expectations.
work.outcome: Average job value nearly doubled within two quarters as smaller jobs filtered themselves out.
work.quote: [A short quote from the client about the result.]

work.name: Client 05
work.line: A physiotherapy clinic that fills its quiet mornings
work.challenge: Afternoons were full and mornings were half empty. The site gave nobody a reason to choose the quiet slots.
work.approach: We tested a morning offer, live availability on the homepage and a shorter booking flow, one change at a time over twelve weeks.
work.outcome: Morning bookings rose 38% and the clinic now runs one fewer locum shift a week.
work.quote: [A short quote from the client about the result.]

work.name: Client 06
work.line: An electrician whose phone number was impossible to find
work.challenge: Most visitors were on a phone, in a hurry, with a problem. The number sat at the bottom of a long page.
work.approach: A click-to-call bar on every screen, emergency and planned work split from the first tap, and pages that load in under a second on 4G.
work.outcome: Phone calls from the site more than doubled in the first two months.
work.quote: [A short quote from the client about the result.]

work.name: Client 07
work.line: An accountancy practice that stopped attracting the wrong clients
work.challenge: The site spoke to everyone, so the team spent hours a week on calls with businesses it could not help.
work.approach: We rewrote the site for the three client types the practice actually serves, with an honest section on who it is not for.
work.outcome: Unqualified enquiries fell by almost half and the partners got their Friday afternoons back.
work.quote: [A short quote from the client about the result.]

work.name: Client 08
work.line: A cleaning company that turned one-off jobs into contracts
work.challenge: Plenty of one-off bookings, very few people coming back. The site never mentioned that regular contracts existed.
work.approach: Contract pricing up front, a follow-up sequence after every one-off job, and a landing page for each type of building they clean.
work.outcome: Recurring contracts rose 57% over two quarters.
work.quote: [A short quote from the client about the result.]

journal.title: Put your prices on your website (yes, even you)
journal.lede: The most common reason service businesses hide their prices is fear of scaring people off. The people it scares off were never going to buy.
body: Every week someone tells us their work is too custom to price. Then, ten minutes later, they describe the three packages that make up most of their invoices. Most businesses have a typical range, they just have not written it down.

A visitor who cannot find a price has two choices: ring and ask, or leave. The ones who ring are often the ones with the smallest budgets, because they have the least to lose. The ones who leave include the client you wanted, who assumed you were either too expensive or not serious.
You do not need a full price list

A starting price is enough. So is a range with a sentence about what moves it. ‘Most kitchen installations land between £9,000 and £16,000, depending on the units and the plumbing’ tells people everything they need to decide whether to call.
Publish a ‘from’ price for each main service
Explain the two or three things that change the price
Say what is not included, so nobody feels misled later
In our experience the enquiries that follow are fewer but much better, and the first call stops being a negotiation.

journal.title: Your contact form is quietly losing you work
journal.lede: Every field you add is a question someone has to feel like answering. Most forms ask far more than they need to.
body: Open your own contact form on a phone and fill it in with your thumb. Count the fields. Notice which ones you would skip if you could. That is the experience your customers are having, usually while doing something else.

To call someone back you need a name, a way to reach them and a sentence about the problem. Everything else, such as budget, timeline and how they heard about you, can wait for the first conversation.
A form that ends with a vague ‘thanks’ leaves people wondering whether it worked. Say who will reply and by when. ‘Rob will call you before 5pm tomorrow’ beats ‘we will be in touch’ every time.
Cut the form to four fields or fewer
Put the phone number right beside it for people who would rather call
Promise a specific reply time, and keep the promise

journal.title: Why the 90 days after launch matter more than launch day
journal.lede: A new website is a guess about what your customers want. The three months after it goes live are when you find out how good the guess was.
body: Launch day feels like the finish line. It is closer to the start. Until real people use the site, every decision is based on interviews, experience and educated assumptions.
We watch three things: where people arrive, where they stop, and what they do just before they get in touch. Session recordings show the moments of hesitation that no analytics dashboard will.
Small changes, one at a time
Most improvements are not dramatic. A clearer button label, a price moved higher up the page, a photo of the actual team instead of a stock image. Made one at a time, each change can be measured.
That is why every project we build includes ninety days of tuning. It is not an upsell. It is the part of the job that turns a nice website into a useful one.

journal.title: Stock photos are costing you trust
journal.lede: People can tell. A slightly blurry photo of your real team does more for you than a perfect photo of strangers in a meeting room.
body: Service businesses sell people. Customers want to know who will turn up, who will answer the phone and whether they seem like the sort of people who do a good job.
You do not need a professional shoot to start. Photos of the team at work, finished jobs and the van outside a client’s house are more convincing than anything from a stock library.
Photograph every finished job before you leave
Use the same light, warm edit on everything so it feels consistent
Replace stock images one at a time, starting with the homepage

journal.title: What our free website review actually covers
journal.lede: A twelve-minute recording, three priorities and a rough idea of what each is worth. Here is exactly what to expect.
body: When you send us your address, one of us opens your site on a phone and on a laptop and records the screen while talking through it. No automated audit tool, no forty-page PDF.
A recording of around twelve minutes
The three changes we would make first, in order
A rough idea of what each change could be worth to you
Nothing, unless you want it to. Plenty of people take the recording, make the changes themselves and never hire us. That is a perfectly good outcome.

contact.faq_lede: Still not sure? Send the form above or ring us. A real person replies within one working day.
faq: Usually within two to three weeks of a signed quote. We take on two new projects a month so each one gets proper attention.
Yes. Most of our clients are elsewhere in the UK and we work remotely with all of them.
What if I only need a few changes?
Book the free review. If a full project is not worth it for you, we will say so and suggest what to do instead.
Who owns the website when it is done?
You do. The domain, the hosting account, the code and every file are in your name from day one.
Can we update the site ourselves?
Yes. Every site comes with an editor your team can use, and a short recorded walkthrough of how to change pages, prices and photos.
What if we don't like the first design?
You see two directions before anything is built. We then revise the one you pick until it is right, inside the quoted price.

sections: Quincy Lou Ltd is a website studio registered in England and Wales. We are the data controller for personal information collected through this website. You can contact us about privacy at the email address at the bottom of this page.

When you use the contact form we collect the details you choose to give us: usually your name, email address, information about your business and your website address. If you sign up for our newsletter we collect your email address. Our hosting provider records standard technical logs such as IP addresses and browser types.

We use your details to reply to your enquiry, to prepare a website review if you ask for one, and to send the newsletter if you subscribed. Our legal basis is your consent or our legitimate interest in responding to people who contact us.

We do not sell your information. We share it only with services we use to run the business, such as our website host, email provider and form handling, and only as far as needed to provide those services.

Enquiries that do not become projects are deleted after 12 months. Client records are kept for as long as the law requires for accounting purposes. You can unsubscribe from the newsletter at any time using the link in each email.

You can ask to see the information we hold about you, ask us to correct or delete it, or object to how we use it. Email us and we will respond within one month. You can also complain to the Information Commissioner’s Office (ico.org.uk).
This site does not use advertising or tracking cookies. If we add privacy-friendly analytics in future, this page will be updated to explain what it collects.
